Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Peter Gill in 2014, the year he directed his play Versailles at the Donmar in London. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian Peter Gill Peter Gill, playwright who turned ordinary lives into extraordinary drama, dies aged 86 Beginning his career as an actor, Gill went on to write plays including The York Realist as well as directing for the Royal Court and National Theatre Mark Fisher Tue 4 Aug 2026 09.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Tributes have been paid to the director and playwright Peter Gill who died on Monday at the age of 86. His agent Mel Kenyon said Gill’s work had a “rare emotional delicacy” and was “beautifully observed and finely tuned” while the director Michael Grandage said Gill’s “contribution to the British theatre will come to be regarded as quietly seismic”. Gill began his career as an actor at London’s Royal Court in 1958 when still in his teens. Over the next six years, he played Silvius opposite Vanessa Redgrave as Rosalind in Michael Elliott’s lauded RSC production of As You Like It, as well as several roles in the British premiere of Brecht’s The Caucasian Chalk Circle. Uncertain of his strengths as an actor, however, he moved into directing. He was encouraged by the Royal Court’s artistic director George Devine who took him on as an assistant director. He would go on to stage as many as 100 productions. The first, in 1965, was A Collier’s Friday Night by DH Lawrence, a writer whom he championed in the following years. He revived the play in 1968 as part of a trilogy of Laurence’s neglected mining plays, adding The Daughter-in-Law and The Widowing of Mrs Holroyd. He also staged The Merry-Go-Round in 1973. In 1976, he became the first artistic director of Riverside Studios in Hammersmith in London, where he staged The Cherry Orchard, with Eleanor Bron, Julie Covington and Michael Elphick, and The Changeling, with Brian Cox and Robert Lindsay. He also established an eye-catching programme of international work. Central to his operation was the Riverside theatre studio, a series of actors’ workshops designed to foster a company spirit. View image in fullscreen Stephen Hagan and Matthew Burton in The York Realist at Riverside Studios in 2009. Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian In 1980, he became associate director at the National Theatre , where, in 1984, he set up the National Theatre Studio to give playwrights and directors space to develop ideas. He remained with the National until 1997. His many productions for the company included Christopher Hampton’s Tales from Hollywood, with Michael Gambon, Billie Whitelaw and Ian McDiarmid; Thomas Otway’s Venice Preserv’d, with Ian McKellen, Michael Pennington and Jane Lapotaire; and Harley Granville-Barker’s The Voysey Inheritance, with Dominic West and Julian Glover. Elsewhere, he staged plays by Chekhov, Pinter, Orton, Shaw, Mamet and Hare. His work as a playwright was no less impressive. His first play, The Sleepers Den, about a family falling apart in a claustrophobic Cardiff slum, was produced in 1965 and starred Eileen Atkins. He returned repeatedly to the working-class Catholic Wales of his childhood, drawing out the extraordinary in ordinary lives and frequently focusing on male relationships, gay or otherwise. Subsequent work included Over Gardens Out, about two teenage tearaways, and Small Change, a coming-of-age tale about two Cardiff boys, which he staged three times over his career. In the Blue, an expressionist play about two gay men, was written in such a way as to make it impossible to know what was real and what was fantasy. In Sheffield in 2002, Grandage devoted a month-long season to Gill’s plays. It included the premiere of Original Sin, about an upwardly mobile Victorian street boy, and a revival of Small Change. Also revived were Kick for Touch, about two brothers, one of whom has had an affair with the other’s wife, Mean Tears, a romantic drama set in the greed-is-good 1980s, and Friendly Fire, aimed at teenagers. The York Realist, staged by English Touring theatre in 2002 before a run in the West End, considered the class system through the lens of an affair between a Yorkshire farmer and a London theatre director. Guardian critic Michael Billington rated it among the best plays of the 21st century. His other later plays included Versailles, As Good a Time as Any and Something in the Air. Gill was appointed OBE in 1980 and reflected on a life of theatre-making in his book Apprenticeship in 2008. Kenyon said that Gill “loved actors and acting” and added: “Whenever we talked, I walked away a wiser person … He was a singular man, a kind, generous and curious man. I will miss him greatly.” Tamara Harvey, co-artistic director of the Royal Shakespeare Company, said that Gill’s “unerring ability to capture the complexity of human existence will live on in his writing but he will, nevertheless, be deeply missed”. Gill is survived by his nieces and nephews. He was predeceased by his brothers Bernard and Paul, and his sister Mary. https://www.budapesttimes.hu/hungary/orb.text: The Budapest Times Orbán rebrands Fidesz as freedom fighters against ‘Tisza autocracy’ Fidesz is declaring a policy of resistance rather than opposition politics, in order to build a new, broad coalition of freedom against the authoritarian system being constructed by the Tisza Party — Viktor Orbán proclaimed on Saturday in Băile Tușnad, during his lecture on the closing day of the 35th Bálványos Summer Open University and Student Camp. Speaking before an audience of several thousand gathered in front of the open-air stage, the Fidesz president assessed that the Tisza Party wants to and is beginning to build a new authoritarian system. In his view, the dismantling of democracy and the rule of law is currently under way in Hungary, in the interest of exercising exclusive power. Viktor Orbán said: “this is a criminal act,” and while it carries no consequences now, “it will matter when we restore the rule of law, and then it will matter greatly.” He indicated that through tailor-made, retroactively applicable legislation, half of the opposition had been “excluded from politics,” and that “through a tailor-made, retroactively applicable constitutional amendment, the President of the Republic was removed, the President of the Constitutional Court was removed, the Prosecutor General was dismissed, and with that, the rule of law was also abolished.” After removing Fidesz from power, the goal is to eliminate Fidesz altogether — to bar its leaders from politics and to make any political alternative impossible through illegitimate decisions, the former prime minister said. He pointed out that the roughly 3.5 million people who voted for Tisza still believe that arbitrary rule will only be used against Fidesz supporters — but they are mistaken. The essence of arbitrary rule, he said, is that power no longer recognizes its own limits, and one day Tisza voters will also wake up to find there is no one to protect them from abuses of power. According to his summary, this new power is aggressive, violent, and abuses its strength. It is not concerned with the affairs of the country but with persecuting the opposition; it is not trying to create unity but is destabilizing Hungary and disrupting social peace, the Fidesz president listed. Viktor Orbán compared the political system being built in Hungary to developments in Venezuela, which he described as a peculiar blend of communist thinking, political arbitrariness, and economic oppression. In his view, those who voted for change in the spring “I don’t think voted for an abuse of their trust.” The majority of them acted in good faith and expected fewer government mistakes and more economic results, he said. He added that after a defeat, one must always look at the world self-critically, but there is little time for that now, because “freedom is in danger in Hungary.” For this reason, the Fidesz chairman declared, the party must shift from an opposition politics built on self-criticism to a politics of resistance. Among the tasks he listed were the persistent refutation of lies spread about Fidesz, informing the public about the threats posed by the economic situation, defending the achievements of the past 16 years, protecting the victims of abuses of power, and building a coalition against autocracy. “Let us stand up for freedom, let us build the broadest possible resistance, let us create the broadest possible coalition in defense of freedom! We must protect Hungary, because we cannot be, to our shame, Europe’s banana republic!” the former prime minister stated. He added that although Fidesz is a political party, it must not concern itself with questions of power at this time — rather, its role is to serve the “national resistance.” In his view, the goal of the national resistance is the restoration of freedom, and freedom is not a matter for any party, nor is it even a question of the left or the right. “Our task is to stand by our two and a half million voters,” the Fidesz chairman declared. Viktor Orbán noted, however, that this was not enough for a majority. The hundreds of thousands still needed to form one would be brought by “the political waves generated by reality,” and together they would form “a new, broad coalition of freedom,” which would secure “a majority in favour of restoring freedom and democracy,” he said. The former prime minister touched on the fact that in April, 53 percent of Hungarians voted for Tisza and 47 percent against it, adding that this ratio would reverse sooner than people might now think. He explained this by saying that the “Tisza autocratic system” lacks the economic foundations to sustain itself. In his view, Tisza voters would soon realise that this was “not the horse they wanted.” Viktor Orbán stressed that Fidesz must now “draw the widest possible arc, with room for every freedom-loving person.” It must operate as an incubator, not strengthening itself but rather the groups of freedom-loving people, he emphasised. “Let us learn from our mistakes! Let us proudly stand by our achievements, strengthen national resistance, and support freedom-loving people! Let us stand by those who raise their voices, and let us guarantee to the people that what will be taken from them through the coming austerity measures will be given back to them by a new, calm, composed civic government! Difficult times are coming, and we will fight,” the Fidesz president concluded his speech at Tusványos. Artificial intelligence was used for the translation of parts of the original Hungarian text. https://business-review.eu/luxury/fine-f.text: Franțuzisme, a Romanian premium artisanal dessert brand, launches with a EUR 66,000 investment Franțuzisme , a Romanian premium artisanal dessert brand, is launching on the local market following a EUR 66,000 investment made through the Bucharest-Ilfov Regional Programme 2021–2027. The investment covered the fit-out of the pastry workshop, the acquisition of professional equipment and the development of the brand, which specializes in handcrafted desserts produced in small batches. Founded by Cătălina Clément, Franțuzisme is a social enterprise built around the belief that a dessert is not simply a product, but an experience, a texture, a memory. Cătălina Clément trained in contemporary dessert artistry with Cédric Grolet, one of the most internationally acclaimed pastry chefs , an experience that contributed to the development of her own dessert concept. “Franțuzisme did not start with a business idea. It started with a question that science does not take into consideration: what do children miss when they grow up without experiencing the authentic taste of a fruit? In looking for the answer and trying to give my daughter that experience, I came to study contemporary dessert artistry with Cédric Grolet and to build a brand that places the experience of the dessert, rather than simply the product itself, at the heart of every creation,” said Cătălina Clément, founder of Franțuzisme. The idea behind Franțuzisme was born from a personal experience of its founder, Cătălina Clément. Her daughter, Amélie, refused to eat fruit, which led Cătălina Clément to wonder what a child misses, beyond the nutritional aspect, when they do not experience the taste of a fruit. The answer began to take shape in December 2022, in Paris, when Cătălina Clément discovered the trompe-l’œil desserts created by Cédric Grolet. Read more about LIH Group returns to positive gross profit after the first half of 2026 and focuses its strategic growth around insurance read more Franțuzisme translates the techniques of contemporary French pastry, developed by master pastry chef Cédric Grolet, into its own approach centred on taste, texture and aesthetics. The products are handcrafted in small batches at the brand’s own laboratory in Tunari. The core collection consists of trompe-l’œil desserts: individual sculptures that replicate the appearance of fruit with remarkable precision, made exclusively from natural ingredients, including fresh fruit, cream and chocolate. The production process is predominantly manual, with each creation going through several stages of infusion, freezing and molding. Small-batch production allows for close control of both the process and the final product, from ingredient selection to presentation. In its first stage of development, Franțuzisme operates as a premium artisanal pastry laboratory focused on small-batch, made-to-order production, with customers collecting their orders directly from the workshop. At the same time, the brand is developing its presence in the private and corporate events segment through dedicated collaborations and customized collections of trompe-l’œil and Fruits givrés desserts, created for weddings, anniversaries, christenings and corporate projects. Franțuzisme is a registered social enterprise, with a social employee and an active social mission. The social component has been integrated into the company’s development model from the very beginning, with part of the team coming from vulnerable communities. Alongside its commercial activity, Franțuzisme plans to organize regular workshops for children from residential care centers in Ilfov County, with the aim of giving them access to creative and culinary experiences. “For us, the social component is not a separate project, but part of how we are building Franțuzisme. We believe that access to beautiful experiences, education and opportunities should not depend on a person’s background. That is why we want the development of the brand to create value both for our customers and for the communities we are involved in,” said Cătălina Clément, founder of Franțuzisme. http://www.indiagazette.com/news/2792885.text: "We remember India with heartfelt gratitude": EAM Jaishankar pays respects at Kolhapur Memorial in Warsaw ANI 06 Sep 2026, 00:27 GMT+10 Warsaw [Poland], September 5 (ANI): External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar on Saturday (local time) paid respects at the Kolhapur Memorial in Warsaw, remembering the refuge provided by India to 5,000 Polish women and children during World War II. In a post on X, after paying his respects at the memorial, Jaishankar said, 'Dispersed around the world, we remember India with heartfelt gratitude.' https://x.com/DrSJaishankar/status/2096184788168118417 'Paid my respects at the Kolhapur Memorial in Warsaw, remembering the refuge provided to 5,000 Polish women & children during World War II. This act of generosity is still fresh in the memory of the Polish people,' he added. Ministry of External Affairs spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal later shared in a post on X, saying, 'EAM @DrSJaishankar paid respects at the Kolhapur Memorial in Warsaw.' https://x.com/MEAIndia/status/2096222592436998183 Jaishankar also visited the memorial of Jamsaheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, popularly remembered as the 'Dobry (Good) Maharaja' of Jamnagar, in Warsaw. Jaiswal, in a post on X, said, 'EAM @DrSJaishankarvisited the Memorial of the 'Dobry (Good) Maharaja' of Jamnagar in Warsaw today.' https://x.com/MEAIndia/status/2096222493447245971 In a post on X, sharing details of his visit, Jaishankar recalled the Maharaja's words, saying,' I am Bapu, the father of all Nawanagaris, including yourselves.' https://x.com/DrSJaishankar/status/2096180262178594979 Jaishankar said, 'Visited the Memorial of the 'Dobry (Good) Maharaja' of Jamnagar in Warsaw today.' He thanked Polish MP Kinga Gajewska and Ochota Mayor Piotr Krasnodebski for joining him. 'Jamsaheb Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja ji is fondly remembered for looking after 1,000 Polish children during World War II. His warmth & compassion remain an abiding bridge between India and Poland,' he added. Jaishankar also shared another post on X featuring a glimpse of his visit to Warsaw, saying, 'A glimpse of my visit to Warsaw #Poland.' Earlier on Friday, highlighting the rapid expansion of the India-Poland Strategic Partnership, External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar said that New Delhi and Warsaw are working on new agreements across cybersecurity, space, clean coal, classified information, and critical minerals. Addressing the press alongside Polish Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosaw Sikorski, Jaishankar reviewed the Action Plan agreed upon during Prime Minister Narendra Modi's visit to Poland, characterising the bilateral progress as highly encouraging. 'Today, Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sikorski and I reviewed the Action Plan that was agreed upon when Prime Minister Modi visited Poland two years ago. The report card that we got was a very solid one, indicating an uptick in trade and investments, deeper defence collaboration, and expansion in traditional areas like mining and energy, as well as new possibilities emerging in space, digital, AI and innovation,' Jaishankar stated. Turning to institutional integration with the European continent, Jaishankar noted that Poland plays a vital role in India's expanding engagement with the European Union and the negotiations for a Free Trade Agreement. 'In the last few years, India's ties with the European Union have deepened very visibly,' Jaishankar said. 'The centrepiece of that is, of course, the free trade agreement, which President Ursula Von Der Leyen described as the mother of all deals. This will open up immense economic opportunities to both nations. As a key member of the European Union, Poland naturally stands to gain in that process.' On Friday, Jaishankar also called on Polish President Karol Nawrocki and held extensive delegation-level talks with Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radosaw Sikorski in Warsaw. The discussions focused on strengthening the India-Poland Strategic Partnership and addressed key global conflicts and emerging geopolitical challenges. With Sikorski, Jaishankar reviewed the implementation of the India-Poland Joint Action Plan 2024-28 across sector-specific areas. Jaishankar was on an official visit to Poland as part of his visit to Ukraine and Poland from September 3 to 5. Composite: Supplied/NSW Supreme Court Australia news Detective breaks down in court as she recalls finding Beau Lamarre-Condon’s alleged murder victims Lamarre-Condon has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies in Sydney in February 2024 Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press Wed 7 Oct 2026 01.47 EDT First published on Tue 6 Oct 2026 22.45 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A detective has broken down in court while describing the moment she found the bodies of two men allegedly murdered by former police officer Beau Lamarre-Condon. Jesse Baird, 26, and his new boyfriend Luke Davies, 29, were shot dead in a Sydney terrace in February 2024. Lamarre-Condon, Baird’s ex and a then-police officer, has pleaded not guilty to murder, arguing the men died in two separate violent struggles after he entered the home disguised as a food delivery rider. Beau Lamarre-Condon trial shown CCTV of accused’s movements across Sydney after alleged double murder Read more His subsequent efforts to dispose of their bodies at Bungonia – 200km south of Sydney – were indicative of his panic about the unexpected deaths, his lawyer has said. A detective who co-ordinated a search of Cella Farm, where Lamarre-Condon allegedly tried unsuccessfully to sink the bodies in a dam, told the alleged murderer’s trial how she eventually found the remains of the two slain men eight days after the shooting. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Detective Senior Constable Christine Abela had been involved in searching the farm, where crime scene officers discovered a padlock had been cut, the jury heard. Prosecutors allege the lock was cut with an angle grinder Lamarre-Condon had asked his friend to buy on the drive from Sydney. Concrete blocks and gym weights were found at the edge of a dam on the farm, the jury was told. On 27 February, Abela was diverted to a Greek monastery about 20km away. “There was a strong smell as soon as I got out of the car,” she told a NSW supreme court jury on Wednesday. “The scent of a decomposing body.” The detective became emotional as prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC took her through her memories of the odour becoming stronger as she approached two blue and silver surfboard bags. The bags were covered with sticks, branches and stones, the detective said. Evidence and testimony in week two of Beau Lamarre-Condon’s trial – video The prosecution alleges Lamarre-Condon became infatuated with Baird after they broke off contact in November 2023, resolving to murder him. However, Lamarre-Condon’s close friend Nicole Harvell told the court on Wednesday she could not remember any conversation with the ex-officer about Baird after the pair broke up for the final time. That was despite her being in almost daily contact with the now-31-year-old. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Senior Constable Harvell recalled trying to contact her friend when she saw media reports that he was under suspicion for the two men’s deaths. “Fuck Beau, are you ok?” she texted to Lamarre-Condon’s phone. She never received a reply. The sworn officer maintained under cross-examination the accused killer had months earlier told her about enlisting his mother to help him lie to Baird. Lamarre-Condon posted an Instagram story with a bunch of flowers and the caption: “When he’s in Melbourne but still sends you these.” But publication was restricted to select friends that did not include Baird. The photo was designed to imply Baird sent flowers to the accused, despite the pair not being in a relationship at the time, Harvell said. When Baird discovered the ruse, Lamarre-Condon spent $160 on a bouquet identical to the photo to lie to Baird, the officer’s friend said. Lamarre-Condon then sent a photo to Baird showing his mother with the fresh bouquet. The bouquet had a handwritten note to imply his mother had been the intended recipient and they were from her partner, who was in Melbourne, the jury heard. “I recall the accused telling me his mother had written that note,” Harvell said. The trial continues.
